description_full: InterContinental Hotels Group PLC owns, manages, franchises, and leases hotels in the United Kingdom, the United States, and internationally. It operates hotels under the Six Senses, Regent, InterContinental Hotels & Resorts, Vignette Collection, Kimpton Hotel, Hotel Indigo, voco, Ruby, HUALUXE, Crowne Plaza, Iberostar Beachfront Resorts, EVEN Hotels, Holiday Inn Express, Holiday Inn, Garner, avid hotels, Atwell Suites, Staybridge Suites, IHG, Holiday Inn Club Vacations, and Candlewood Suites brand names. The company also provides IHG Rewards loyalty program. InterContinental Hotels Group PLC was formerly known as Six Continents PLC and changed its name to InterContinental Hotels Group PLC in June 2003. The company was founded in 1777 and is headquartered in Windsor, United Kingdom.
ceo_bio: Mr. Elie Wajih Maalouf | CEO & Executive Director | Age 61 | Compensation: $4.7M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 13K people. Revenue per employee of $398K ranks in the above the sector median among Consumer Cyclical peers, improving at 14%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $67K of free cash flow annually. CEO compensation is 12× revenue per employee (reasonable relative to workforce productivity).
financial_summary: Intercontinental Hotels Group is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $26.1B market cap on $5.2B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +10% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size. Operating margins are contracting by -2.5pp, the first warning that competitive pressure is eroding the franchise.
Returns on capital run at 68% against a 8% cost of capital — a 60-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $870M in free cash flow — roughly 17 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.18× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.4× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 5.9×.

Shareholder yield of 4.5% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 23% operating margin runs 16pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (8%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.80x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 29% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 1% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 25% and a beta of 0.88, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.28 vs 5y 0.86), so read it loosely.
About $31.3M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 59% in the 2020 crash, 33% in the 2022 bear market and 64% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $95.21 (margin of safety -88%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 43%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $72.81 to $127 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 38.0 vs 19.3, EV/EBITDA 125.5 vs 11.2 and P/FCF 29.9 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 58% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.3% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 0.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 5 covering analysts target $154 on average, 14% below the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 68% clears the cost of capital of 8.4% by 60pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.23).
It converts 17% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.18x.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.4x net debt to EBITDA ($1.1B of cash against $4.2B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 5.9x.
The current ratio of 0.98 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 10.1% over 3 years and 16.7% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 51%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 51.0% a year over five years.
Analysts expect 11.8% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 11%.
It returns 4.5% a year to shareholders (3.4% in buybacks and 1.1% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.6% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 13,049 employees, each generates about $398K of revenue, in line with the Consumer Cyclical median, and productivity has risen 14.3% a year.
That works out to $67K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.7M (12x revenue per employee).
